articles.title_orig: Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis, scarred by Oct. 7, see only a threat
articles.title_zh: Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis, scarred by Oct. 7, see only a threat
articles.content_orig:
SDEROT, Israel — One by one, Israelis peered through the tourist-style binoculars at the shattered Gaza town of Beit Hanoun, a distance of several football fields away, where buildings tilted in the rubble like broken teeth. The only noticeable movement was dust kicked up by Israel’s military.
The Israelis squinted for a few moments and gestured others over. The lookout is a rare place where they can confront the Palestinian territory firsthand, and some celebrate its devastation.
An Israeli documentary released this year included one onlooker exclaiming, “Wow, destroyed beautifully.” The Associated Press heard similar sentiments there.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people in southern Israel and abducted 251 others, leading to a devastating war and, eventually, a fragile ceasefire.
Three years on, a visit to the communities attacked that day made clear: It’s too soon for many residents to see the Palestinians next door as anything other than a threat.
The highway running parallel to Gaza, where militants gunned down people trying to flee, is dotted with memorials. Victims’ smashed and bullet-pocked cars are assembled elsewhere, rusting and piled a half-dozen high. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a potential attack were disregarded, mark their deaths that day.
One resident, Deganit Bar Hay, said she still can’t barbecue because the smell of burnt flesh — “the smell of hell” — is a trigger.
Globally, there is shock and condemnation over how Israel has conducted the war, and how Gaza remains in ruins and cut off from the world a year since the ceasefire. Over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, and the vast majority of its 2 million residents live in rat-infested tent camps or among the debris.
But empathy for them is still unthinkable for many in Israel, with memories raw. Israeli media report little on the Palestinians of Gaza, and Israelis rarely if ever hear their voices unless they seek them out.
A new Israeli documentary, “NAZA,” in which military insiders describe what they said was the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, has sparked outrage at the filmmakers, not the government. Everywhere in Israel — at train stations, beaches, the Gaza viewpoint — are dozens of stickers in memory of the hundreds of soldiers killed on Oct. 7 and in the ensuing war.
“We are post-traumatic, all of us,” said Ziporah Livneh, outside a cafe catering to tour groups and soldiers a short drive from Gaza. Much of her family died in the Holocaust, and she came to Israel at the age of 2.
Now, she said, the answer for Gaza is to keep believing in people’s humanity but respond strongly to acts of evil. A society and a country can’t be built on revenge, but for the world to think “we can be Mother Teresa, it is a hypocrisy.”
Many Israelis are still turned inward. They say their story isn’t being heard or understood. They assert that Palestinians in Gaza receive more attention, even as Israel’s government still prevents journalists from entering the territory except under rare, highly managed visits — and very few Palestinians can leave.
From the day the war began, Israeli news and hearts were focused on the dead and the hostages taken into Gaza, a land that despite being an hour’s drive from Tel Aviv has long felt remote. Cross-border contact had been severely limited since Hamas seized power in 2007. Then, on Oct. 7, militants ripped the fence apart.
This is the first anniversary since the attack that all remaining hostages are out of Gaza, alive or dead.
There is rebuilding in the Israeli communities where militants went home to home, burning and shooting. There is also the insistence on keeping Oct. 7 memories alive, with hope that the outside world will come to understand how Israel’s sense of security was smashed.
“I know many people around the globe don’t understand us,” said Mor Izreal, director of an Oct. 7 virtual reality exhibit in the border city of Sderot. She said over 10,000 people have visited since it opened a year and a half ago, most from overseas. Reactions range from sadness to rage to connectedness, she said.
This year, for the first time since the attack, there is also an election, a momentous and angry one.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is deeply divisive. Many Israelis accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7 attack and not securing the hostages’ release sooner, before many of them were killed. He is also accused of corruption and threatening democratic institutions.
But there has been little criticism of how his government has treated the Palestinians in Gaza, where Israel’s military now controls over 60% of the territory, squeezing them into an ever-smaller space.
Next to a bullet-pocked rocket shelter outside Sderot, a man held a banner calling for an official inquiry into the security failures surrounding the attack. Netanyahu has long resisted one.
Amit Gurfinkel said he spent Oct. 7 in a safe room with his daughter in the nearby community of Netivot, holding a knife and expecting the worst.
Gurfinkel is a minority in a population that has long supported Netanyahu. Posted across Sderot are campaign banners for his far-right allies, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir — the national security minister who has called for killing “30 to 40” people in targeted assassinations in Gaza each night.
Security is paramount, especially in Sderot, where residents have just 10 seconds to seek shelter when rockets are fired from Gaza. But Gurfinkel sees Israel’s reputation as crucial, too. He shook his head over passing drivers who shouted their support for Netanyahu, whose government is isolated over the destruction in Gaza and who has been issued an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court.
“This is pathological. I don’t know,” Gurfinkel said. “Sociologists and psychologists will have answers in the years to come.”
Some Israelis argue there are no real civilians among Palestinians in Gaza, pointing to Hamas’ entrenchment. Some Palestinians feel the same way about Israelis, noting that military service is mandatory for most Jewish men and women.
“Death to Arabs” is written inside a rocket shelter across from the Sderot police station that was besieged and then destroyed. “Hamas is still in Gaza” is scrawled on a guardrail on the highway where bodies spilled from vehicles on Oct. 7. “Make Gaza Jewish Again” is on a banner in a public square in Jerusalem’s Old City.
There is little public discussion about how everyday Palestinians are doing after three years of war.
“I think about them, and it’s complicated,” Adi Marmelstain said of the people in Gaza. She was visiting the sprawling memorial for the Nova music festival, where hundreds of people were shot dead on Oct. 7.
Her 20-year-old daughter, a member of the security forces like many young Israelis, stood in shorts and a tank top, her rifle slung across her. Both knew people who had been killed.
Marmelstain recalled waking up another daughter on Oct. 7 and sending her to war with bottled water and cookies. She later asked herself what she had been thinking. Three years later, life is not much easier to contemplate.
The world doesn’t see Israel in the right light, she said. And the Palestinians in Gaza?
“I think they have the right to live, but they choose not to,” she said.
Associated Press video journalist Alon Bernstein in Sderot, Israel, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Man Accused in Cornell Sex Assault Wants James Removed as Prosecutor
articles.title_zh: Man Accused in Cornell Sex Assault Wants James Removed as Prosecutor
articles.content_orig:
A newly formed Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees announced today that it has retained former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Yates, a partner at law firm King & Spalding LLP, to lead a comprehensive independent review of how the University prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus.
The review will examine Cornell’s policies, practices and resources across the full range of prevention and response, including how reports are received and investigated; how students are supported; how hearings, disciplinary decisions and appeals are handled; the role, processes and response of campus police; coordination with other law enforcement agencies and prosecutors; campus safety reporting; and policies and oversight involving fraternities, sororities and other student organizations. It will also examine the Board’s oversight of these issues.
As part of that broader mandate, Yates and her team will conduct a detailed review of the University’s response to the allegations involving Jane Doe and members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter.
The Special Committee is comprised of Chair of the Board of Trustees, Anne Meinig Smalling, and fellow trustees, Jennifer L. Davis, Tara Holm, Howard L. Morgan Ph.D., Beckie Robertson, Stephen C. Robinson, Esq., Martin F. Scheinman, Esq., and Robert W. Selander.
“Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work,” said Anne Meinig Smalling, Chair of the Special Committee. “The questions raised by the Jane Doe matter warrant a rigorous examination of Cornell’s response to that case, but our responsibility is broader. We have asked Ms. Yates and her team to examine Cornell’s overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer.”
The review will assess Cornell’s practices against applicable requirements under Title IX, the Clery Act, the Violence Against Women Act’s Campus SaVE Act and New York State law, as well as recognized best practices in higher education for preventing and responding to sexual misconduct.
Yates and King & Spalding will have full independence in conducting the review and will report their findings and recommendations directly to the Special Committee. The University will provide the investigative team with access to relevant policies, records, case files, personnel and leadership, consistent with applicable law and privacy requirements. The review will assess Cornell’s organization, staffing and resources; policies and procedures; student support services; investigative and adjudicative processes; discipline and remediation; relationships with outside support organizations; and law-enforcement practices and coordination.
Smalling continued: “It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others. We want to understand not just what happened in 2024, but how Cornell can become a leader in preventing sexual violence, supporting those who come forward and responding to allegations rigorously, fairly and compassionately.”
Yates is a former Acting Attorney General and Deputy Attorney General of the United States and a longtime federal prosecutor. She is a partner in King & Spalding’s Special Matters and Investigations practice and has extensive experience conducting independent investigations for boards and institutions. She previously led U.S. Soccer’s independent investigation into allegations of abusive behavior and sexual misconduct in women’s professional soccer.
The Special Committee has asked Yates and her team to conduct the review as expeditiously and thoroughly as possible. The Board intends to share the results and recommendations with the Cornell community.

articles.title_orig: Russell calls world record, engagement a perfect close to 2026
articles.title_zh: Russell calls world record, engagement a perfect close to 2026
articles.content_orig:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Olympic champion Masai Russell said she knew she had the speed to break the 100-meter hurdles world record. She just did not know what it would feel like when it happened.
“When I ran the 12.09, I was just like, wow,” the former Kentucky athlete said in a sit-down interview with WKYT.
Russell clocked 12.09 seconds on Aug. 27 at the Diamond League meet in Zurich, Switzerland, shaving three-hundredths of a second off Tobi Amusan’s 12.12. The wind reading was 0.0 meters per second. Amusan, the previous record holder, finished second in 12.23. Nadine Visser was third in 12.34.
She closed the season by winning the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship, taking the 100-meter hurdles title Sept. 11 in Budapest in 12.22. Amusan was second again, in 12.34, and Visser third in 12.39.
The Zurich run was the centerpiece of a season in which Russell went unbeaten in Diamond League competition, winning all seven of her races and the Diamond Trophy. She is the reigning Olympic gold medalist from the Paris Games.
Russell said competition still pulls something different out of her. She said she studies athletes and performers who take on another persona in their field, naming Michael Jordan and LeBron James.
“I see what people say. I see the doubters. I see the haters,” she said. “I also see, of course, all the love that I get, too. So, you know, you see it all. But I think for me, I love proving people wrong.”
The world record has not changed the target. Russell said she wants to stay at the top of the podium every year.
“I just wanna continue every single year, just being one of those people that’s always at the top of the podium, that’s always winning, that’s always dominating, and really just, like, looking like the Usain Bolt of the women’s 100 hurdles,” she said.
The year has not been only about the track. Russell said she and longtime boyfriend Robbie Springfield, a former Kentucky athlete, are engaged. She announced the engagement last weekend.
“It’s just a beautiful way to top off such a great year, such a great season,” Russell said. “Robbie’s been a huge, huge, huge part of my success, like, on the track. So yeah, I mean, beautiful way to top off this 2026 season, no lie.”

articles.title_orig: California woman accused of spying for China will be jailed while awaiting trial
articles.title_zh: California woman accused of spying for China will be jailed while awaiting trial
articles.content_orig:
LOS ANGELES — A California woman accused of acting as a Chinese spy inside the U.S. will remain jailed pending her trial after a judge sided Wednesday with federal prosecutors who argued that she poses a flight risk.
Wanying Zhang, 34, who sometimes goes by Heather, will remain in pretrial detention following the ruling by U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim. The FBI arrested her Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she could board a flight to China.
In a criminal complaint, prosecutors accused Zhang of spying on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his residence in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. Zhang, of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of downtown Los Angeles, hadn’t registered as a foreign agent as required, they said.
Zhang was represented in court Wednesday by veteran criminal defense attorney Craig Harbaugh, who argued she wouldn’t flee in part because of her strong family connections to Southern California, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said.
Zhang’s family had been willing to put up their home equity — valued at $700,000 — combined with bonds from her husband, his sister, his father and a family friend totaling $120,000 as an assurance that she would appear in court.
But prosecutors countered that she had “hundreds of thousands of dollars available to her” in China, as well as investments in a business and contacts that could allow her to flee easily.
“I don’t think it’s a very strong argument that she’s that tied to her family here,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Amanda Elbogen said, casting Zhang as a lying foreign agent with the skills and resources to evade detection and capture.
An investigation found Zhang attended China’s University of International Relations, which an FBI investigator said in court documents is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus.”
The charging document alleges Zhang had been communicating with a former classmate, who is now believed to be a Chinese official, through whom she had arranged an agreement to conduct surveillance of the Taiwanese president’s son. The document says she later captured photos, video and license plate information about him and sent them to her alleged Chinese handler.
She is alleged to have done all of that alongside an unidentified “Individual 1,” according to the complaint, who prosecutors said Wednesday had already fled to China two weeks ago.
Zhang wore a white jail jumpsuit and remained shackled for the entirety of Wednesday’s proceedings, a departure from her initial appearance Monday, when she was uncuffed and wore street clothes, with her hair neatly styled.
Wednesday’s hearing had several testy moments among prosecutors, Harbaugh and Kim, largely over whether Zhang’s pattern of one-way flights overseas was a credible defense that she wasn’t a flight risk and whether she had other U.S. properties to rely on for monetary assets.
Discussion in court revealed Zhang had disclosed only one residence to pretrial services, while her husband later revealed they owned two more, which her attorney said was a misunderstanding.
“She lied to pretrial services. She’s a real estate agent; she should know what properties she owns,” Elbogen countered.
Zhang is due back in court as early as Oct. 19 for a preliminary hearing — if federal prosecutors don’t indict her before then.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: CNBC Daily Open: Another Fed hike is on the horizon — but when?
articles.title_zh: CNBC Daily Open: Another Fed hike is on the horizon — but when?
articles.content_orig:
Hello, this is Justina Lee writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to another edition of CNBC's Daily Open.
Meeting minutes released Wednesday showed that U.S. Fed officials expect interest rates to increase before year-end, but the meeting summary provided no indication of when specifically it would happen.
The U.S. Treasury selling $39 billion of 10-year notes in an auction knocked yields off their highs, while the S&P also pulled back from its record high on Wednesday.
South Korean tech giant Samsung posted a third-quarter preliminary operating profit that exceeded 100 trillion won for the first time in its history, while Lululemon poached Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger.
Traders are bracing themselves for another hike from the U.S. Federal Reserve this year, after meeting minutes released Wednesday showed that Fed officials expect to increase interest rates before the end of the year in order to fend off inflation that has run above target for more than five years.
However, the meeting summary did not show when the hike would occur – only that a stable labor market and persistently higher prices would likely lead to a second hike this year. Rates will be decided by the Fed on Oct. 28 and then again on Dec. 9.
Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury yields backed off their highs after the Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes in an auction. According to BMO, the sale was "strong," with higher than average bidding from non-dealers.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield reached its highest level since April 2002 at 5.365% on Wednesday. The 30-year bond yield also hit its highest level since May 2002 at 5.732%.
Meanwhile, the S&P also pulled back from its record high on Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.66%, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.22%. The Nasdaq Composite was 0.22% lower.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 0.92% lower. South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 2% and Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat. Mainland China market remained closed for the Golden Week holiday on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the spotlight is back on South Korea's tech sector, after Samsung Electronics posted a third-quarter preliminary operating profit of 107.40 trillion won ($80.2 billion). This is the first time in its history that the company has exceeded 100 trillion won, propelled by booming AI demand. Samsung is expected to release its full third-quarter earnings, including a breakdown by business division, later this month.
In the consumer sector, Lululemon said Wednesday that Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger is joining the company as president and chief product officer , with effect from later this month. The news comes as the athleisure space becomes increasingly competitive.
Over in the oil markets, concerns over supply disruptions slightly eased, after member states of the International Energy Agency agreed to help address rising fuel prices by prioritizing the release of diesel stocks .
Trump doesn’t think Russia plague incident is bioweapon, plans Putin call Wednesday
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. does not think the death of a Russian laboratory worker from a suspected case of plague is the result of a bioweapon.
Trump also said he planned to call Russian President Vladimir Putin , who turned 74 on Wednesday, later in the day. Trump previously had said that call would focus on the plague-related incident.
Trump's comments came at an Oval Office event promoting Trump Accounts , the new tax-deferred savings and investment accounts that more than 60 million American children under age 18 have been automatically enrolled in.

articles.title_orig: Trump returns to Texas, where Republicans are struggling
articles.title_zh: Trump returns to Texas, where Republicans are struggling
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in less than a month to stump for a Senate candidate who’s privately questioned his political capital and whom the president has publicly insulted in personal terms.
Such is the final sprint to the November 3 midterm elections as the GOP faces an increasingly uphill battle to hold on to the Senate, with the path to the majority running through Texas.
Republicans are pouring millions into bolstering state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who polls have shown is facing a closer-than-expected race against Democrat James Talarico in a state Trump carried by more than 13 points in 2024 and that hasn’t elected any Democrats statewide since 1994.
Trump’s Wednesday appearance in San Antonio, one Texas GOP strategist said, will be closely watched in the coming days for whether it can improve Paxton’s standing — which could determine continued investment in the state.
The president’s latest Texas trip — which comes less than a week after his last stop here — is part of an aggressive midterm travel blitz that has taken him to traditional red strongholds he overwhelmingly won two years ago, including Alabama, Oklahoma and Nebraska. The president has repeatedly told his rally crowds to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this fall, and his advisers believe their best hope for November is boosting base turnout .
But some Republicans , even in these red states, are looking for distance from the unpopular president. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott will not be at Trump’s Wednesday evening rally, citing scheduling conflicts. He skipped last week’s Trump appearance too.
“It’s pretty clear to me the Paxton team has made the calculation that they believe it’s absolutely worth it,” the Texas GOP strategist said.
But as Trump arrived Wednesday, Paxton is also making headlines for seeming to blame the president and some of his agenda for his struggles.
The GOP nominee told a group of donors and lobbyists last month that the Iran war and high gas prices are hurting his campaign, according to audio obtained by Axios on Wednesday. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said, according to Axios. CNN has not independently verified the audio.
Paxton’s campaign dismissed the story. “The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” spokeswoman Madison Cercy told CNN in a statement, adding that Trump “is doing everything he can to bring prices down.”
But that followed The New York Times last week publishing audio of Paxton complaining that Trump’s midterm convention, held last month in Dallas, wasn’t helpful.
“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” the Texas attorney general said. In a statement to CNN, Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux called the Times story “manipulated nonsense” to “create a story that doesn’t exist.”
Paxton has been plagued by his own set of scandals , including securities fraud charges, which ended in a pre-trial agreement; allegations of infidelity; and a 2023 impeachment in the state House (the Senate acquitted him). But that baggage didn’t stop Trump from backing Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.
Their relationship, however, has appeared fraught, even as Trump told reporters in the Oval Office earlier Wednesday that he has no regrets about backing Paxton.
At a stop in Denton, Texas, last week, the president called Paxton “one of the most loyal people” — but also “a pain in the ass sometimes.”
Then there’s his frequent ribbing of the state attorney general’s appearance.
“Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said during a speech at the Dallas convention: “I don’t.”
Trump did not repeat that refrain Wednesday night, calling Paxton a “fantastic man” as the two showcased warm relations on stage.
“I’m very proud of him and I think he’s gonna be an unbelievable senator,” Trump said as he invited Paxton to speak.
Paxton, in turn, expressed gratitude to his guest. “Aren’t you guys glad he came to San Antonio?” he asked an enthusiastic crowd.
The president “understands how important Texas is to efforts to try to keep the Senate in Republican control, so I think he can put all that aside and probably focus on the bigger picture,” said one Texas GOP operative unaffiliated with the Paxton campaign, granted anonymity to speak freely.
“But I’m sure he enjoys making Paxton squirm at the same time,” the operative added.
Asked about the candidate’s relationship with Trump earlier Wednesday, Paxton’s campaign pointed to his planned appearance on stage with the president.
Paxton’s comments reported by the Times underscore how the president’s unpopularity — his approval rating is 34% in the latest CNN Poll of Polls — may make him an unwelcome guest for some candidates.
And he is losing support among a group that helped propel him to victory in 2024. His approval rating among Latino voters was just 27%, according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll earlier this week. Trump may be looking to turn that tide with his visit to San Antonio, where the population is 64.6% Hispanic or Latino.
Trump sought to juice turnout among his MAGA base Wednesday evening with a focus on border security and other red meat issues. He attacked Talarico as a vegan — a claim the Democrat has denied. And there were visible efforts to organize, including information about early voting and mail-in ballots for attendees on screens and in handouts.
But Trump’s visit, the Texas Republican strategist said, comes with its own risk.
“Why go where you can potentially motivate the other side, rather than going to places like Lubbock or Amarillo or East Texas, where you can try to use that brand to actually motivate, you know, the type of voter that needs to turn out for Paxton to win?” the strategist said.
There were some signs of discontent. At least a dozen protesters, who interrupted Trump’s rally on several occasions, were removed from the event.
And Democrats see Trump’s return to Texas as a good sign for their side.
“If you have to pull in Donald Trump four times in the closing stretch of the campaign in Texas, then you have given up on independent voters. This is a loss mitigation strategy,” said one Texas Democratic operative.
The Senate race — and the GOP primary and runoff leading up to it — is already on track to be one of the nation’s most expensive.
The GOP-aligned bill in Texas is expected to exceed $300 million, with the party and its affiliated groups outspending Democrats by more than 5-to-1, CNN has previously reported . Since the end of the GOP runoff in late May, Republicans have spent $158 million on ads, with an additional $38 million in upcoming ad reservations, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Democrats, meanwhile, have spent about half that: $75 million on ads between late May and Tuesday, with $6 million reserved.
But that level of spending in deep-red Texas comes with consequences for the rest of the Senate map.
“A lot of us are very disappointed that our predictions have proven correct, and it’s going to cost somewhere between $100 and 200 million to save Ken Paxton as the Senate nominee,” said a Texas GOP strategist who had raised  concerns about Paxton during the state’s primary.
“If we save Ken and lose the Senate majority because we’ve lost Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Iowa and Ohio, the Monday morning quarterbacking is going to be biblical,” they added.
But Texas has seen close Senate races before, with Democrats’ hopes dashed at the ballot box. Eight years ago, Trump was a key surrogate for Ted Cruz when the senator faced then-rising Democratic star Beto O’Rourke. Cruz, unencumbered by the personal baggage Paxton is carrying this year, won his race by just 2.6 points.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Launches $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra to Take on MacBook Pro
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Launches $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra to Take on MacBook Pro
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft today announced launch timing and pricing for the Surface Laptop Ultra that it unveiled earlier this year.
The 15-inch Surface Laptop Ultra is priced starting at $2,599, undercutting Apple's $2,999 16-inch MacBook Pro , and it targets the same creator and developer market. Microsoft says it is built for "demanding creative, software development, AI, engineering, and 3D workloads."
Microsoft's new laptop uses an Nvidia RTX Spark chip, which includes an Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores and an Nvidia Grace CPU with up to 20 cores. It supports up to 128GB of unified memory and has a new thermal architecture to support the hardware. The RTX Spark is an Arm-based chip, so the laptop runs Windows on Arm with x86 apps using Microsoft's Prism emulation.
According to Microsoft, the Surface Laptop Ultra is its most powerful notebook to date. It has the "brightest, sharpest, and most vivid display" Microsoft has used in a Surface device, with peak HDR brightness that's 25% higher than the M5 ‌MacBook Pro‌'s. The mini-LED display is a touchscreen, and it supports gestures and navigation, but not pen input.
The laptop is lighter than the 16-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌, with a large haptic trackpad and upgradeable storage. Microsoft even adopted a MagSafe equivalent, adding support for Magnetic Connect. Microsoft says Magnetic Connect is the "world's first built-in magnetic USB-C charging on a laptop." The device has three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, an HDMI port, an SD card reader, and a 3.5mm headphone jack.
Along with the Surface Laptop Ultra, Microsoft announced the $5,999 Surface RTX Spark Dev Box to compete with devices like the Mac Studio and Mac mini . It is equipped with an Nvidia RTX Spark chip and offers up to 1 petaflop of AI performance with support for AI models up to 120B parameters.
Microsoft is offering a bonus to customers who "break up" with their MacBooks. MacBook owners can get up to $1,000 cash back when purchasing a Surface Laptop Ultra by trading in an eligible MacBook. The Surface Laptop Ultra launches on October 16.
"We're confident that once today's creators and developers experience everything Surface Laptop Ultra has to offer, they won't look back," reads Microsoft's website.
The Surface Laptop Ultra will directly compete with Apple's rumored OLED MacBook, which could also have an Ultra name. The MacBook Ultra is expected to feature a touchscreen, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and a thinner and lighter design.

articles.title_orig: Mamdani draws bipartisan backlash for criticizing Israel on Oct. 7 anniversary
articles.title_zh: Mamdani draws bipartisan backlash for criticizing Israel on Oct. 7 anniversary
articles.content_orig:
Israelis gathered in vigils across the country to remember the terror attack’s victims. In New York City, anti-Israel groups rallied and Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s post on the attacks drew criticism.
A group of anti-Israel protesters on Wednesday targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , calling him a "traitor," accusing him of "genocide" and claiming he "cannot weaponize being brown anymore."
The crowd of more than 100 demonstrators marched from City Hall to Union Square, where a vigil was held to mark the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks in Israel. The vigil was organized as an evening of mourning for those killed in the Oct. 7 attacks and the bloodshed that followed, including Israelis and Palestinians.
The anti-Israel crowd was just outside the barricades of the Israelis for Peace Vigil, beating on drums and attempting to drown out the speakers, according to City & State New York.
Mamdani was at the vigil and held a candle as protesters threw various insults at him, including accusations of genocide and "selling all your people out."
ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'
A group of anti-Israel protesters targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him a "traitor." (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)
"Zohran, what do you say? How many kids did you kill today?" the protesters shouted, according to the outlet.
"700,000 dead. Mamdani, your hands are red!" they also chanted.
"Traitor, traitor, come on out! You sold all your people out!" the group was also heard chanting.
The crowd also shouted: "Zohran, you can’t hide. We charge you with genocide!"
"We don’t care about where you’re from. You cannot talk about being Muslim anymore. You cannot weaponize being brown anymore. Identity politics can only get you so far," they said.
One protester also claimed to be a former intern for Mamdani, saying the mayor "was never working for the people."
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stands at a rally called by Israelis for Peace. (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)
Protesters also demanded that Mamdani take action against New York real-estate events that have marketed properties in Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which the demonstrators characterize as "stolen" Palestinian land, according to City & State New York.
"Mayor Mamdani, take a stand. Stop the sale of stolen land," the group chanted.
The protesters also called for abolishing the City University of New York's Board of Trustees, whose members are largely appointed by the mayor and governor. Protesters have previously accused the board of ignoring demands to divest investments linked to Israel and criticized its handling of anti-Israel demonstrations on campus.
Despite the protesters' accusations of genocide on Wednesday, Mamdani is a longtime critic of the Israeli government's actions in Gaza and has denounced its treatment of Palestinians in the aftermath of the 2023 attack.
MAMDANI SAYS IT WAS 'STRANGE' GETTING CALLED OUT BY NETANYAHU AFTER CALLING FOR HIS ARREST
An anti-Israel crowd was just outside the barricades of the Israelis for Peace Vigil, beating on drums and attempting to drown out the speakers. (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)
In a statement on Wednesday, Mamdani condemned Hamas’ attack as a "horrific war crime" while also characterizing Israel’s subsequent military operation as a genocide.
"The suffering did not begin nor end that day," he wrote. "It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children."
Israel has rejected accusations that it is committing genocide in Gaza, saying its military targets Hamas and other terrorist groups while seeking to minimize civilian casualties.
The mayor's statement sparked bipartisan backlash , with Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., calling it "egregious and insulting."

"There are 364 days of the year to focus on that. This is a day that should just be focused on what was by all agreement a horrific terror attack," Goldman, who is Jewish, told Politico. "What the mayor’s statement did today was to blame Israelis for the attack that they suffered three years ago. Regardless of what you actually think of the conflict and what’s happened either since or before, there’s no excuse for victim blaming."

articles.title_orig: Mamdani criticized by fellow Democrats for statement mourning Oct. 7 attacks while condemning Israel
articles.title_zh: Mamdani criticized by fellow Democrats for statement mourning Oct. 7 attacks while condemning Israel
articles.content_orig:
A statement by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani that recognized three years since Hamas' "horrific" attack on Israel — and extensively criticized Israel's "ongoing genocide" in the Gaza Strip — has drawn fury from some Democrats.
Mamdani is a longstanding and vehement critic of Israel's actions during its war with Hamas in Gaza, and an opponent of U.S. aid to Israel — issues that have divided Democrats nationwide and drawn criticism for the mayor from moderates, leaders of Jewish groups and Israeli officials. Mamdani has long defended his stance, saying criticism of Israel is distinct from antisemitism.
Wednesday's statement by Mamdani began by calling it a "profoundly painful" day for many New Yorkers, noting Hamas' "horrific war crimes" on Oct. 7, 2023 , including the killing of about 1,200 people in Israel and the taking of more than 250 hostages. He added: "We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss."
The mayor then shifted to criticizing Israel for its "devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza" — noting the more than 74,000 deaths recorded in the enclave, according to the Hamas-controlled Gaza Health Ministry .
"Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes," Mamdani said.
"Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment," Mamdani added.
Several Democratic elected officials blasted Mamdani's statement, arguing it was too focused on Israel rather than Hamas.
Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida accused Mamdani of "desecrating the memory of murdered, innocent Jews," Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey said the mayor was "blam[ing] the victims" of the Oct. 7 attack, and Jersey City Mayor Steven Fulop called the statement "inappropriate and unnecessarily inflammatory."
Rep. Richie Torres, a Democrat who represents the Bronx, penned an X post that did not name Mamdani, but said: "Perhaps, for just one day—October 7th—the critics of Israel could take a vacation from their hysterical hatred of the world's only Jewish State and find it within themselves to express condolences for the thousands of Israelis murdered, maimed, mutilated, raped, and abducted at the hands of Hamas."
Rep. Daniel Goldman — who lost a Democratic primary in his Manhattan and Brooklyn district to Mamdani-endorsed Brad Lander earlier this year — called the mayor's message "reprehensible."
"In the guise of 'grieving' with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with," Goldman wrote on X.
Lander, the Democratic nominee in Goldman's deep-blue district, wrote a statement of his own on Tuesday that condemned Hamas but argued against the "flattening of empathy."
"We can mourn for those lost on October 7th and still acknowledge the enormous imbalance of power between Israel and the Palestinians," Lander wrote in a post on Substack.
Mamdani also faced pushback from the Anti-Defamation League, whose CEO, Jonathan Greenblatt, is a frequent critic of the mayor. Greenblatt wrote on social media that in Mamdani's statement, "not once do you say 'Jews.'"
"You are weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points," Greenblatt wrote.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called Mamdani's statement an "outrageous & disgusting rant," while Ofir Akunis, Israeli consul general in New York, called it a "disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered."
CBS News has reached out to Mamdani's office.
Mamdani's stance on Israel has drawn intense scrutiny — and applause from his allies — since he began his unexpected ascent to the mayor's office.
Ahead of the 2025 Democratic mayoral primary, Mamdani vowed that if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited New York City, he would seek Netanyahu's arrest on an International Criminal Court warrant accusing him of war crimes.
Over the summer, Mamdani conceded that the city did not have the power to execute the warrant. The U.S. is not a party to the global treaty that created the ICC and generally does not recognize its authority. Israel has called the war crimes allegations "absurd and false."
When Netanyahu visited the city last month to address the United Nations General Assembly, he accused Mamdani of antisemitism and said "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
"Shame on you for distorting the facts, shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor, shame on you for spitting in the face of truth," Netanyahu said.
Mamdani has long rejected allegations that his strong criticisms of Israel have fueled antisemitism, and says the city "has no room for hate or bigotry of any kind."
Last month, Mamdani unveiled a plan to combat antisemitism , including a dedicated antisemitism hotline and funding to upgrade security at synagogues.
Asked by CBS News New York about the criticism he has faced and whether he believes he should dial back his statements, Mamdani said last month : "I think criticism of a prime minister, criticism of government policy is distinct from bigotry of a people. … And what my job is to ensure is not only that we are proud of being the most Jewish city in the United States of America, but that we also make this a city where Jewish life can continue to flourish."

articles.title_orig: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.title_zh: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.content_orig:
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case
Russia has dismissed media reports of a second suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia, as the World Health Organization (WHO) urged Moscow to formally respond to its inquiry regarding the reports.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that “the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information”, in response to a question about reports of a second case.
Peskov said that information on the suspected cases should be derived from official statements by Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
Russia’s health regulator said there were no infections detected among staff after a plague institute worker died from pneumonia. The origin of the illness remains unknown, prompting international concern that the case could involve the plague.
Russia acknowledged on Sunday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk died after she was diagnosed with a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, prompting global concern over a suspected plague case.
The United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Russia to be transparent about the situation.
US President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked whether it’s possible the infection was from a bioweapon, “We do not think so.”
“They are saying it is very much under control,” he said, adding “Russia is not saying much either.”
Trump confirmed he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and when asked about what US intelligence agencies are reporting, Trump said the two sides are “in very deep discussions” and that they would likely be able to provide an update “probably tomorrow.”
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia to clarify “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause” at the Irkutsk institute.
“We have received information from two media outlets, one of them is Russian,” Tedros said in a briefing on Wednesday, adding, “We asked Russia to respond to that.”
“We cannot ignore any reporting that comes,” the WHO chief said.
WHO Director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said the UN agency does not know the “causative agent” behind the death in the first suspected case.
In a briefing, Van Kerkhove said, “We don’t understand how she was infected.”
“We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow-up of the questions that we have asked,” she added.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) described the risk to the United States from the suspected pneumonic plague case as “extremely low”.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said on Wednesday that the US agency is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State, Defense and other agencies to monitor people travelling from the area.
The CDC has a health station at New York City’s John F Kennedy International Airport that can screen travellers coming from the Siberian region, she added.
About 200 people per year travel from the Siberian region to the United States, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.
Direct flights between Russia and the US have been suspended since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.
“What we’re doing from a whole of government standpoint is we’re making sure that we understand exactly what that threat is,” Schwartz said at the Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Health event in Washington, DC.
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC said in a separate statement.

articles.title_orig: Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says
articles.title_zh: Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says
articles.content_orig:
Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, GACA reported.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.
GACA said it is working “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities” to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
New cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport.
On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swathe of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones against Aden airport early on Wednesday. No casualties were reported.
Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

Jacob Coxon alleges Beijing can close any technological gap with the US as it has ways to ‘steal our progress at any time and catch up’
“Right now, if we just stopped, they would try and catch up. But I think one really important thing people don’t realise is that China already has spies at OpenAI and Anthropic,” Coxon said.

articles.title_orig: The World Figure and Fancy Skating Championships return to Lake Placid
articles.title_zh: The World Figure and Fancy Skating Championships return to Lake Placid
articles.content_orig:
The World Figure and Fancy Skating Championships are back in Lake Placid this weekend.
The Olympic sport combines figure skating with artistic expression, while it uses a unique canvas.
Skaters create artistic designs on the ice with their blades and technique.
Ice is painted black making way for the art to be created and seen.
Skating legends from the past and current professionals come together to create different patterns on the ice.
This year, the performances will include something the world championships have never seen before.
"This year there is a live improvisation to live musicians of which you're going to see skaters and performers, world class performers who've never actually skated the routine before at that moment in front of the audience," said Karen Courtland Kelly, a former U.S. Olympian and Chef De Mission of the World Figure Sports Society. "It's never been done in a World championship, but we're going to do it for the first time ever in Lake Placid with live improvisation to live music."
The championships start Thursday, Oct. 8, and wrap up on Sunday, Oct. 11.

articles.title_orig: A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop
articles.title_zh: A thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with feedback loop
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
The laser-accessible nuclear transition in the thorium-229 isotope has been identified as a candidate for realizing an optical nuclear clock 1 that might outperform current optical clocks based on electron-shell transitions in atoms or ions 2 . It is expected to be more robust against external perturbations 3 , 4 and to provide enhanced sensitivity in clock-based tests of the fundamental principles of physics 5 , 6 . Here we realize a thorium-229 nuclear clock by stabilizing a continuous-wave laser to the 148-nm nuclear transition with rapid feedback based on absorption spectroscopy 7 . The thorium-229 nuclei are embedded in a millimetre-sized, room-temperature calcium fluoride crystal. A subharmonic of the 148-nm radiation is continuously compared with a Yb + single-ion clock. The nuclear clock shows a shot-noise-limited fractional frequency instability of \(3\times 1{0}^{-12}/\sqrt{\tau /{\rm{s}}}\) where τ is the averaging time, approaching 10 −15 instabilities over 1 day of operation. Improvements to the instability by several orders of magnitude are projected for future devices. We use the nuclear clock to constrain models of ultralight dark matter by searching for periodic fluctuations and slow drifts in the nuclear transition energy, on timescales between 20 s and 1 day. Benefitting from the enhanced sensitivity of the thorium-229 transition, these constraints compete with the best atomic clocks concerning dark matter coupling to photons and go beyond previous measurements regarding coupling to the strong force.
Over the last 70 years, atomic clocks based on microwave and optical electronic transitions have successfully served as frequency standards based on their high levels of stability and accuracy 2 , 8 , 9 , 10 . To elevate these atomic timekeeping devices to the next generation, in 2003, Peik and Tamm 1 proposed a nuclear clock based on the extraordinarily low-energy isomeric state of the thorium-229 ( 229 Th) isotope at 8.4 eV. With a lifetime approaching 1 h for a bare nucleus in vacuum, this transition offers a potential resonance quality factor of the order of 10 19 (ref. 11 ). Additionally, the nucleus couples only weakly to perturbative fields 12 , which allows the construction of an optical clock implemented in a solid material at room temperature 13 . By doping microgram amounts of 229 Th into a crystal host, an experimentally simple and robust clock can be created, offering a large gain in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared with approaches based on a single or a few isolated nuclei, while only moderately degrading the resonance quality factor 1 , 4 , 11 , 14 .
A clock based on the 229 Th nuclear transition is of great interest for testing theories beyond the Standard Model of particle physics that indicate that the fundamental constants vary over time 5 . The low energy of the 229 Th isomer transition originates from a coincidental near-cancellation of the mega-electronvolt-scale Coulomb and nuclear contributions to the binding energies of the 229 Th ground and excited states, making the transition frequency highly sensitive to fluctuations in the coupling constants of the interactions involved 5 , 6 , 15 . As a result, a solid-state nuclear clock in its development phase would already be competitive with or may even surpass the sensitivity of advanced comparable atomic clocks in the search for dark matter.
The realization of a nuclear clock builds upon half a century of scientific discoveries. See the reviews in refs. 12 , 16 . In a research stream initiated by Kroger and Reich in 1976 (ref. 17 ), the energy of the 229 Th nuclear transition was narrowed down from an originally conjectured value of below 100 eV to −1(4) eV (ref. 18 ), 3.5(1.0) eV (ref. 19 ) and then 7.8(5) eV (refs. 20 , 21 ) using gamma spectroscopy. Using the internal conversion decay channel, the existence of the 229 Th isomer was proven in 2016 (ref. 22 ) and the energy value refined to 8.28(17) eV (ref. 23 ). An optical detection of the 229 Th radiative nuclear decay was realized in 2022, which determined the isomer energy to be 8.338(24) eV (ref. 24 ) in the vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) range. Thereafter, resonant laser excitation in Th:CaF 2 , Th:LiSrAlF 6 crystals and ThF 4 and ThO 2 thin films was reported in 2024 and 2025 (refs. 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ), quickly followed by the resolution of the nuclear quadrupole structure in Th:CaF 2 (refs. 13 , 29 ).
The development of 148-nm continuous-wave laser systems in 2025 (refs. 30 , 31 ), in combination with highly doped 229 Th:CaF 2 crystals 32 , 33 , has enabled the measurement of the nuclear transition with absorption spectroscopy 7 . With this technique, it became possible to probe the 229 Th nuclear transition continuously, without being limited by the long isomeric state lifetime of approximately 10 min. Moreover, absorption provides a higher detection efficiency, yielding three orders of magnitude more signal photons per second compared with fluorescence.
An optical clock is based on an atomic transition with a narrow linewidth, which is probed by a clock laser with a long coherence time. By stabilizing this laser to the atomic resonance, it can inherit the desired stability and reproducibility from the atom. Aiming for millihertz resolution and accuracy, the feedback times in this process typically extend to several seconds, requiring a pre-stabilization of the laser for higher-frequency noise to an optical cavity that has a suitable short-term stability. With the combination of these two control loops, very stable laser frequencies can be generated and then converted into a time signal through a frequency comb acting as an optical clockwork 34 .
Here, we transfer this concept from an atomic to a nuclear reference transition. Although previous studies 7 , 13 , 14 demonstrated that it is possible to excite the 229 Th nucleus using VUV lasers stabilized to external frequency standards, it has not yet been possible to construct a system in which the laser interrogating the 229 Th nuclei is steered by the nuclear transition itself. Our system is a nuclear clock that operates as a stand-alone device.
The nuclear clock is composed of a cavity-stabilized laser for short-term stability (referred to as the clock laser) and a 229 Th interrogation system providing long-term stability (Fig. 1a ). We use a continuous-wave VUV laser source to interrogate the 229 Th nuclei 7 , 30 . This laser source comprises a 1,187-nm frequency-quadrupled commercial laser (the seed laser in Fig. 1 ) and a single-pass second-harmonic-generation stage using a randomly quasi-phase-matched strontium tetraborate (SBO) crystal. The frequency and linewidth of the 1,187-nm interrogation laser are determined by an offset phase lock to the clock laser. We modulate the offset lock frequency to perform absorption measurements. For the clock laser, we use a high-finesse cavity-stabilized external-cavity diode laser operating at 1,187 nm. The stabilization of the clock laser to the cavity uses a Pound–Drever–Hall scheme on a sideband generated by an electro-optical modulator, allowing us to shift the frequency of the clock laser independently of the cavity resonances.
a , Thorium-229 nuclear clock at TU Wien. It comprises an external-cavity diode laser (ECDL), which serves as a clock laser stabilized to a high-finesse cavity through the sideband of an electro-optical modulator (EOM), and a seed laser, which is frequency-quadrupled, followed by the last SBO-based VUV frequency generation doubling. The seed laser is modulated through the offset lock to generate the error signal from the

articles.title_orig: World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF
articles.title_zh: World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF
articles.content_orig:
Recovery of tigers, tuna and green sea turtles show nature loss can be reversed when action taken, charity says
Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.
The World Wildlife Fund ( WWF ) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.
Nature loss is no longer just an environmental challenge but a direct threat to the global economy, the report says, noting that about half of global GDP – roughly $58tn (£44tn) in 2023 – depends on nature and its ecosystem services. The authors write that species collapse now poses an “existential threat to economic stability, geopolitical security and human wellbeing”.
Animal populations were found to be falling most sharply in tropical, biodiversity-rich regions, while trends in northern temperate parts of the world appeared much gentler.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, land and freshwater wildlife populations fell by an average of 95% between 1970 and 2022, while the equivalent declines were 80% in Africa and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.
Freshwater wildlife suffered the sharpest losses across the world’s ecosystems, with monitored populations in rivers and lakes down by an average of 85%, compared with 69% for land species and 59% for marine species.
Tanya Steele, the chief executive of WWF UK, said: “Nature loss is not just a crisis for wildlife. It’s already sending us the bill through growing risks to our food security, water supplies, economy and resilience to climate shocks.
“We stand at a fork in the road: either we continue paying the rising price of nature loss, or we invest in nature’s recovery and a future where people and wildlife can thrive together.”
But despite the pattern of global biodiversity decline, wild tigers, green sea turtles and bluefin tuna are recovering, the report said, showing that “it is still possible to reverse the global loss of nature when action is taken”.
In 2010, about 3,200 wild tigers remained globally and the species was sliding toward extinction. After sustained and targeted conservation interventions, the population has grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%.
Becci Day, WWF UK’s tiger lead, said the remarkable comeback of wild tigers demonstrated the “science of hope” and proved that when climate and ecological action was taken, change was possible.
The report said Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna populations, which were collapsing after decades of overfishing, had now recovered to the point where neither was now considered threatened.
Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever downlisted from endangered to “least concern” on the IUCN red list, reflecting 50 years of coordinated conservation work across about 80 countries.
Dr Mike Barrett, the chief scientific adviser for WWF UK and a co-author of the report, said: “These are examples that show that nature can recover even when pushed right to the brink, and they provide us with inspiration. It’s also very clear that conservation alone cannot tackle the scale of threats facing nature.”
He said nature would have no chance of recovery if “negative tipping points ” – self-reinforcing, irreversible ecological changes that accelerate climate crisis – were passed. “The systems which drive nature’s loss have to be transformed. And that’s energy, food and finance,” he said.
“Our report shows that we’ve already passed the tipping point in the energy sector with the take-up of renewable energy . That transition is now unstoppable. It’s not happening fast enough, but it is unstoppable.”
Humanity must likewise adapt the way it produces food, he said. “Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and therefore the loss of biodiversity. It’s also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and so helps drive climate change, so you have that feedback.”
Dr Steve Smith, a research fellow at Global Systems Institute and a co-author of the report, said: “The biggest prize for nature recovery would be a sustainable and healthy food system, but it’s currently the farthest away from positively tipping. For example, agricultural expansion drives almost 90% of deforestation worldwide.”
Positive tipping points are thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.

articles.title_orig: Webull Stock Falls 20% Over China Ties: Who Really Controls the App?
articles.title_zh: Webull Stock Falls 20% Over China Ties: Who Really Controls the App?
articles.content_orig:
Digital investment platform Webull , which counts 28 million global users , is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to U.S. finance, according to a bipartisan congressional panel's findings shared exclusively with CNBC.
The bipartisan House Select Committee on China in its new report being released Wednesday found "a profound gap" between Webull's public marketing as "an American company" and actual control of the St. Petersburg, Florida-based firm.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the committee found.
The panel asserted that national security concerns around the company have "escalated" since October 2025, when Webull began carrying customer cash directly, according to a regulatory filing the panel cited. The committee alleges that creates a "structural exposure of billions of dollars in American capital."
The committee said the company's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. And those laws in China can compel firms to cooperate with the government in myriad ways, including data transfers.
Webull took issue with the report, saying via a spokesperson, "It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull." "Webull's U.S. business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida and its office in New York City, while U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S.," the spokesperson said via email. "We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide."
Webull's stock plummeted 18% in morning trading.
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., told CNBC in a statement that Webull's "China-based operations put American investors and their data at risk."
"Using technology providers in mainland China and an opaque China-linked ownership structure, Webull exposes its data to our foremost adversary," said Moolenaar, who chairs the House committee that issued the report. "Investors should heed this information when choosing who they do business with."
Webull, which trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange, says it operates a "global network of licensed brokerages," offering investment services in 18 markets around the globe. The online brokerage says it provides retail and institutional investors with 24/7 access to global financial markets. Users of the platform can trade global stocks, exchange-traded funds, options, futures, fractional shares and digital assets on the service.
Former Alibaba and Xiaomi manager Wang Anquan founded Webull in 2016 . Its competitors include Robinhood , Charles Schwab and E-Trade .
The congressional committee, which had requested information from the company in 2024, said Webull represents a national security risk because "critical backend systems, personnel and data flows may remain exposed to the Chinese Communist Party's mandatory intelligence laws and coercive demands."
The committee said in its report that Webull Financial's "intricate corporate and technology framework" is tethered directly to China.
Webull Corp. is a Cayman Islands-incorporated holding company, and the report found it holds $24.6 billion in customer assets. And although the company has a U.S. holding company known as Webull Holdings (US) Inc., the report says the company's technology structure also includes Webull Technologies Pte. Ltd, which is a Singapore-based entity. And the report says Webull uses a mainland China-based subsidiary that supports technology development and platform operations. The company traces its origins to Hunan Fumi Information Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese company that originally launched the business.
The release of the report comes on the heels of a largely friendly summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in September, and it comes ahead of further meetings between the two leaders later this year. It reflects concerns on Capitol Hill that the Chinese government could be planting seeds inside the U.S. financial system that could later be used to disrupt the American economy in the event of further conflict.
The committee also alleges Webull misrepresented the number of its China-based employees. In the report, the committee said the company initially told the committee it "does not have any offices or employees based in the PRC," and that "all Firm employees are located in the United States." But the committee says the firm remains operationally concentrated in China, with its mainland subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, growing to 863 employees, or 62% of the company's global workforce.
_src_links: Webull Stock Falls 20% Over China Ties: Who Really Controls the App?

articles.title_orig: María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87
articles.title_zh: María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87
articles.content_orig:
Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis
‘Now is the moment’: housing activists at Madrid encampment pin wary hopes on Spain’s early election
María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.
News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain, was evicted from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than seven decades.
The pensioner, whose apartment had been purchased by an investment firm who sought to hike her rent by 230%, swiftly became a symbol of the many left behind by Spain’s surging housing market.
Scenes of the eviction, which saw police use rounds of teargas as they carried out the order, made headlines across Spain. The shocking images – showing Abascal being forcibly removed from her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police – swiftly crystallised into anger.
About 10,000 people took to the streets of Madrid hours later, wielding signs such as “Shame” and “We’re all Maricarmen”. From Spain’s north to the south, people poured into plazas to protest the suffering wrought by rents that had soared 80% in the span of a decade while house prices had climbed 63%.
From the hospital where she was being treated for severe exhaustion, Abascal cheered on the fledgling movement. “I would like to be there with you all,” she said in a video shot from her hospital bed. “But I’m not that lucky. So from here, I ask you all for courage and to fight and defend what is yours.”
As encampments began springing up across the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return. The deal did little to quell the anger that had boiled over in the wake of the eviction.
This week the wave of outrage led the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap general election after rightwing and far-right parties voted down two emergency decrees his government had proposed to address the housing crisis.
The Madrid tenants’ union said the solution had come too late for the octogenarian. “This was a completely preventable situation following an agonising ordeal,” it said in a statement announcing that Abascal had died in hospital, reportedly hours before she was due to sign a new lease with the investment firm that had evicted her.
“The events triggered by the injustice of her eviction undoubtedly mark a turning point in the history of this country: massive demonstrations, encampments in the squares, an early election, and the call for a general strike,” it added. “The housing debate is at the center of it all, but the cost of getting to this point has been too high.”
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”
Spain’s health minister, Mónica García, said Abascal’s plight had “served to awaken awareness across all of Spain, lighting a fuse that cannot be put out”, and adding that her “ dignity and courage ” had shown the way.
The Podemos MEP and former equalities minister Irene Montero was more blunt. “This isn’t a death; it’s a murder,” she wrote on social media. “Such bloody anger. Thank you for fighting, Maricarmen.”
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP) – which voted against last week’s emergency housing measures – also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”
Her death came a day after Sánchez’s cabinet approved two new housing decrees intended to “maintain the spirit” of the two previous decrees that were voted down in parliament last week by the PP, the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party.
The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; regulating room rentals; imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases; and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.
With the lower and upper houses of parliament dissolved following the calling of the snap election, the decrees will be voted on by the permanent council of congress, a special council that operates when parliament is not in session.
The body’s 69 members are distributed proportionally among the various parliamentary groups to reflect the composition of the lower chamber, meaning Sánchez will probably have enough support to get at least one of the decrees passed.
In the heart of Madrid, where campaigners have set up a giant protest camp , news of Abascal’s death was met with a moment of silence. Soon after, hundreds marched from the camp to the country’s parliament chanting: “Maricarmen lives on, the fight continues.”

articles.title_orig: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.title_zh: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported.
The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS.
US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny.
The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan ​which brought the charges.
Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports.
Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges.
Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York.
The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.
The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term.
Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States".
Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.
